etymology: Hebrew Abdon, “service” or “servile,” a Pirathonite of Ephraim who judged Israel after Elon.
biblical_def: Abdon the son of Hillel, a Pirathonite of the tribe of Ephraim, was one of the minor judges of Israel, who judged the nation eight years after Elon the Zebulonite (Jdg 12:13). Scripture records of him chiefly his prosperity and his household: he had forty sons and thirty nephews, that rode on threescore and ten ass colts, a mark of wealth and dignity in that age (Jdg 12:14). When he died he was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the mount of the Amalekites (Jdg 12:15). The dictionary marks Abdon among the quiet judges, of whom the sacred history tells little, who delivered and ruled Israel in the long unsettled days between Joshua and the kings. He stands within the great pattern of the book of Judges, that when the people were oppressed, the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them (Jdg 2:16). Abdon was such a raised-up deliverer, set in his place by God for his appointed season. His prosperity is named without praise or blame; what the dictionary draws from his brief record is the faithfulness of God, who in every generation, even the obscure ones, did not leave His people without a ruler and a deliverer of His own providing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithfulness of God in the days of the judges, who did not leave His people without a deliverer even in the obscure generations. When Israel was spoiled, the LORD raised up judges to save them; and Abdon, of whom so little is told, was such a raised-up ruler. His quiet record teaches that God’s providence works through unremembered men as truly as through famous ones, and that no generation of His people is left without the rule and the care He has appointed.

etymology: Hebrew Shammah, perhaps “astonishment” or “waste,” one of the three chief mighty men of David.
biblical_def: Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite was one of the three mightiest of David’s mighty men, remembered for a single deed of valour at a piece of ground full of lentils. The Philistines gathered into a troop where the ground was, and the people fled before them; but Shammah stood in the midst of the ground, and defended it, and slew the Philistines, and the LORD wrought a great victory (2Sa 23:11; 2Sa 23:12). The dictionary marks Shammah as the man who would not flee. The field was small and the lentils a mean prize, and the rest of the people thought it not worth the risk; but Shammah held his ground, and God gave a great deliverance through one man who would not yield his post. So the Scripture teaches the saint to watch, stand fast in the faith, quit himself like a man, and be strong (1Co 16:13), and having done all, to stand (Eph 6:13). The victory is named the LORD’s, for it was God who wrought it; yet He wrought it through a man who stood when others fled. Shammah is a witness that there is no post so small that God cannot win a great victory there, and that faithfulness in a mean field, held against the foe, may be the occasion of a deliverance for the whole people of God.
webster_summary: One of David’s three chief mighty men, who alone defended a field of lentils against the Philistines.

etymology: Hebrew Benayah, “the LORD hath built,” the son of Jehoiada, a mighty man and captain over David’s guard.
biblical_def: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, of Kabzeel, was one of the most valiant of David’s mighty men and the captain of his bodyguard. The Scripture records his exploits: he slew two lionlike men of Moab, and went down and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow, and killed a mighty Egyptian with the Egyptian’s own spear (2Sa 23:20). But his greater honour was his unwavering loyalty to the rightful king. When Adonijah sought to usurp the throne, it was Benaiah who, with Zadok and Nathan, brought Solomon down to Gihon to be anointed (1Ki 1:38), and when Solomon was established, the king set Benaiah over all the host in the room of Joab (1Ki 2:35). The dictionary marks Benaiah as the union of valour and loyalty. His courage was the courage of the righteous, who are bold as a lion (Pro 28:1), and it was bent not to his own advancement but to the service of God’s anointed king. He neither flinched from the lion in the pit nor faltered in his allegiance to the throne God had appointed. Benaiah teaches that true valour is loyal valour, spent in the cause of the rightful King; and his name, “the LORD hath built,” befits a man whose strength was given him to build up the kingdom of God’s choosing.
webster_summary: A mighty man of David and captain of his guard, valiant and loyal, who anointed Solomon king.

etymology: Hebrew Tsadoq, “righteous” or “just,” the faithful high priest under David and Solomon.
biblical_def: Zadok was the faithful high priest in the days of David and Solomon, whose name fitly means “righteous.” When Absalom drove David from Jerusalem, Zadok and the Levites bore the ark out of the city to follow the king, until David sent them back to keep it in its place (2Sa 15:24). When Adonijah sought the throne, Zadok stood with the rightful succession, and it was he who took the horn of oil out of the tabernacle and anointed Solomon, while all the people cried, God save king Solomon (1Ki 1:39). For this fidelity his house was confirmed in the priesthood, and the prophet Ezekiel honoured the sons of Zadok, the priests the Levites that kept the charge of God’s sanctuary when the children of Israel went astray, as those who should come near to minister unto the LORD (Eze 44:15). The dictionary marks Zadok as the pattern of the faithful priest. His loyalty in the day of revolt, and the steadiness of his house through the apostasies of Israel, made him a figure of the faithful priest the LORD promised to raise up, who should do according to that which is in His heart and mind, walking before His anointed for ever (1Sa 2:35). That promise found its full answer in Christ, the great High Priest, of whose unfailing faithfulness Zadok was a shadow.
webster_summary: The faithful high priest under David and Solomon, who anointed Solomon and whose house kept the priesthood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithful priesthood. Zadok stood with the rightful king in the day of revolt, anointed Solomon, and kept the charge of the sanctuary when Israel went astray; and his house was confirmed in the priesthood for its fidelity. He is a figure of the faithful priest the LORD promised to raise up, who should do all His will and walk before His anointed for ever. That promise is fulfilled in Christ, the great High Priest, of whose unfailing faithfulness Zadok was but a shadow; and the believer rests not in any earthly priest but in Him.

etymology: Hebrew Ish-bosheth, “man of shame,” a son of Saul set up as a rival king against David.
biblical_def: Ishbosheth was a son of Saul, set up by Abner, the captain of Saul’s host, as king over Israel at Mahanaim after the death of Saul, in rivalry to David whom God had chosen (2Sa 2:8). He was a weak man, ruling only at Abner’s will, and his short reign was a doomed resistance against the purpose of God. The Scripture sums up the matter in a single verse: there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David, but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker (2Sa 3:1). When Abner forsook him and was slain, Ishbosheth’s hands were feeble, and all the Israelites were troubled (2Sa 4:1); soon after, he was murdered upon his bed. The dictionary marks Ishbosheth as the figure of a kingdom raised against the anointed of God, which cannot stand. His very name, “man of shame,” tells the end of every throne set up against the LORD’s choosing. For God is the judge: He putteth down one, and setteth up another (Psa 75:7); and the house of Saul, however long it warred, must wax weaker and weaker against the king after God’s own heart. So every power that lifts itself against the true Son of David is doomed to the same slow and certain decline.

etymology: Hebrew Uriyyah, “the LORD is my light,” a Hittite by birth and one of David’s faithful soldiers, the husband of Bathsheba.
biblical_def: Uriah the Hittite was one of David’s mighty men, a faithful soldier and the husband of Bathsheba, whom David wronged in the darkest deed of his reign. When David had sinned with Bathsheba and sought to hide it, he called Uriah home from the war, that he might go down to his house; but Uriah, in his soldierly integrity, refused, saying, The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house? as thou livest, I will not do this thing (2Sa 11:11). Unable to cover his sin by Uriah’s faithfulness, David wrote to Joab to set Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle and retire from him, that he might be smitten and die (2Sa 11:15); and so the loyal soldier was slain. But the eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good (Pro 15:3), and the prophet Nathan laid the murder bare: thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword (2Sa 12:9). The dictionary marks Uriah as the faithful man wronged by the great, whose integrity shines the brighter against the king’s sin, and whose innocent blood was not hidden from God, but avenged in the chastening of David’s house.
webster_summary: A faithful soldier of David, husband of Bathsheba, murdered by the king’s plot to hide his sin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the eyes of the LORD are in every place, and the innocent blood of the wronged is not hidden from Him. David, the man after God’s own heart, fell into murder to cover adultery; but Nathan laid it bare, thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and the chastening fell heavy on David’s house. Uriah’s soldierly faithfulness is honoured, and his innocent blood avenged; and the great are warned that no power or place can hide a wrong from the God who beholds the evil and the good, and who will surely require the blood of the faithful at the hand of the mighty.

etymology: Hebrew Gad, “fortune” or “troop,” a prophet who served as David’s seer.
biblical_def: Gad was a prophet of the LORD who served as David’s seer, a counsellor who brought the king the word of God in days of distress and of sin. He was with David in the cave in the days of Saul’s pursuit, and he stood by the king through his reign. When David sinned in numbering the people, the word of the LORD came to Gad, David’s seer, with the offer of three judgments (2Sa 24:11; 1Ch 21:9), and David, choosing, said, Let us fall now into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; let me not fall into the hand of man (2Sa 24:14). It was Gad who afterward directed the king to rear an altar in the threshingfloor of Araunah, where the plague was stayed. His prophecies and the acts of David were written in the book of Gad the seer (1Ch 29:29). The dictionary marks Gad as the faithful prophet at the king’s side, who spoke the word of God to the throne, even the hard word of judgment, and would not flatter the king he served. He stands for the office of the prophet to bring God’s word to the great, unbought and unafraid; and his ministry teaches that the truest friend of a ruler is the man who tells him the will of God plainly, that he may humble himself and fall into the merciful hand of the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew Shemayah, “the LORD hath heard,” a prophet in the days of Rehoboam king of Judah.
biblical_def: Shemaiah, called the man of God, was a prophet in the days of Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when the kingdom was rent in two. When Rehoboam gathered a great army to make war against the ten tribes that had fallen away to Jeroboam, the word of God came to Shemaiah, saying, Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren the children of Israel: return every man to his house; for this thing is from me (1Ki 12:24); and the people hearkened to the word of the LORD and turned back. Again, when Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem because Judah had forsaken the LORD, Shemaiah came to the king and the princes and said, Thus saith the LORD, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak (2Ch 12:5). And when they humbled themselves, saying, The LORD is righteous, the word of the LORD came again, that He would grant them some deliverance (2Ch 12:7). The dictionary marks Shemaiah as the prophet whose word restrained the king from a sinful war and called him to humble himself under the chastening hand of God. His ministry teaches that the word of God by His prophet is to be obeyed though it crosses the will of kings, and that the humbling of a people under rebuke turns away the fulness of wrath and brings some measure of deliverance.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the prophet whose word restrained a king and called a people to humble themselves under chastening.
corruption_paragraphs: Shemaiah has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the prophet who turned Rehoboam from a sinful war and called him to repentance. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the power of the word of God by His prophet to restrain even kings.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the word of God is to be obeyed though it crosses the will of kings, and that the humbling of a people under rebuke turns away the fulness of wrath. Rehoboam hearkened and turned back from war; and when Judah humbled itself under Shishak, the LORD granted some deliverance. So the dictionary honours the prophet’s office to restrain and to rebuke, and draws the lesson that they who humble themselves under the mighty hand of God find His wrath stayed and His mercy stirred.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the LORD hath heard,” Shemaiah names a prophet of Rehoboam’s day.
roots_lines: Shemaiah — Hebrew Shemayah, “the LORD hath heard.”

He announced deliverance when the king humbled himself.
usage: Like Shemaiah, the prophet’s word restrains kings and calls them to humble themselves.

etymology: Hebrew Iddo, perhaps “timely” or “his witness,” a seer and prophet-historian in the days of Solomon and his successors.
biblical_def: Iddo was a seer and prophet in the days of Solomon, Rehoboam, and Abijah, remembered chiefly as one of the prophet-historians whose writings recorded the acts of the kings. The Chronicler appeals to his books again and again: the rest of the acts of Solomon were written in the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam (2Ch 9:29); the acts of Rehoboam in the records of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer concerning genealogies (2Ch 12:15); and the acts of Abijah in the story, or commentary, of the prophet Iddo (2Ch 13:22). His writings have not come down to us as separate books, but the Spirit who moved him gathered the substance of such prophetic records into the canon of Scripture we have. The dictionary marks Iddo as one of the prophet-historians by whom God kept the record of His dealings with His people, for the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost (2Pe 1:21). His labour teaches that the history of God’s people is sacred history, written by men whom He inspired, and that the keeping of the record of His acts is itself a prophetic office; for the Scriptures are not the bare annals of men but the inspired witness to the works and ways of God among His people.
webster_summary: A seer and prophet-historian whose writings recorded the acts of Solomon, Rehoboam, and Abijah.

Now the acts of Rehoboam, first and last, are they not written in the book of Shemaiah the prophet, and of Iddo the seer concerning genealogies? And there were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.
And the rest of the acts of Abijah, and his ways, and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.

corruption_paragraphs: Iddo has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as one of the prophet-historians the Chronicler cites. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the prophetic office of keeping the record of God’s acts among His people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the history of God’s people is sacred history, written by men whom He inspired. The prophecy came not by the will of man, but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost; and the keeping of the record of God’s dealings, as Iddo and Shemaiah and Nathan kept it, was itself a prophetic office. The Scriptures are not the bare annals of men but the inspired witness to the works and ways of God, and the dictionary honours the prophet-historians by whom that witness was preserved against the day it should be gathered into the canon.

etymology: Hebrew Hanani, “gracious” or “the LORD is gracious,” a seer who rebuked Asa king of Judah.
biblical_def: Hanani was a seer in the days of Asa king of Judah, and the father of Jehu the prophet. When Asa, late in his reign, leaned upon a league with the king of Syria rather than upon the LORD, Hanani came to him and said, Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand (2Ch 16:7). And he spoke the great word that has comforted the faithful in every age: For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew Himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward Him (2Ch 16:9). But Asa, once a godly king, was wroth with the seer, and put him in a prison house, in a rage with him because of this thing (2Ch 16:10). The dictionary marks Hanani as the bold prophet who reproved a king and suffered for it, and whose word stands as a perpetual encouragement to trust in God alone. His rebuke teaches that the LORD seeks out the perfect heart to bless and to uphold, and that to lean on an arm of flesh is to forfeit His strength. His imprisonment teaches that the fear of man bringeth a snare, but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe (Pro 29:25); and that even a godly man, when crossed, may turn against the truth that would have saved him.
webster_summary: A seer who rebuked Asa king of Judah for trusting in Syria rather than the LORD, and was imprisoned for it.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the bold seer who reproved a king for trusting an arm of flesh, and suffered for the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Hanani has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the seer who rebuked Asa and was imprisoned. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark his bold reproof and the great word he spoke of the LORD’s searching eyes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD seeks out the perfect heart to uphold, and that to lean on an arm of flesh is to forfeit His strength. The eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show Himself strong for them whose heart is perfect toward Him; and Asa, leaning on Syria, did foolishly and earned wars. The seer’s imprisonment teaches further that even a godly man, when crossed by the truth, may turn against it in his anger; for the fear of man and the pride of a king brought a snare, and Asa, who began so well, ended by oppressing the prophet who told him the truth.
